{{Short description|Generalisation of convexity}}

{{about|the generalisation of convexity used in the calculus of variations|the unrelated generalisation of convexity used in microeconomics|Quasiconvex function}}

In the [[calculus of variations]], a subfield of mathematics, '''quasiconvexity''' is a generalisation of the notion of convexity. It is used to characterise the integrand of a functional and related to the existence of minimisers. Under some natural conditions, quasiconvexity of the integrand is a necessary and sufficient condition for a functional
<math display=block >\mathcal{F}: W^{1,p}(\Omega, \mathbb{R}^m) \rightarrow \R \qquad u \mapsto \int_\Omega f(x, u(x), \nabla u(x)) dx</math>
to be [[Semi-continuity#Lower_semicontinuity|lower semi-continuous]] in the [[weak topology]], for a sufficient regular domain <math display=inline> \Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d </math>. By compactness arguments ([[Banach–Alaoglu theorem]]) the existence of minimisers of weakly lower semicontinuous functionals may then follow from the [[Direct method in the calculus of variations|direct method]].<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Rindler
 |first=Filip
 |title=Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer International Publishing AG
 |series=Universitext 
 |year=2018
 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-77637-8
 |isbn=978-3-319-77636-1
 |page=125
}}</ref>
This concept was introduced by Morrey in 1952.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Morrey 
 |first1=Charles B.
 |author-link=Charles B. Morrey Jr.
 |year=1952
 |title=Quasiconvexity and the Lower Semicontinuity of Multiple Integrals
 |journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics
 |volume=2
 |issue=1
 |pages=25–53 
 |publisher=Mathematical Sciences Publishers
 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1952.2.25
 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/pacific-journal-of-mathematics/volume-2/issue-1/Quasi-convexity-and-the-lower-semicontinuity-of-multiple-integrals/pjm/1103051941.full
 |access-date=2022-06-30
|doi-access=free
 }}</ref> This generalisation of convexity should not be confused with the [[polysemy|polysemetic]] concept of a [[quasiconvex function]].

==Definition==
A locally bounded Borel-measurable function <math display=inline> f:\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> is called quasiconvex if
<math display=block> 
\int_{B(0,1)} \bigl(f(A + \nabla \psi(x)) - f(A)\bigr)dx \geq 0
</math>
for all <math> A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d} </math>  and all <math> \psi \in W_0^{1,\infty}(B(0,1), \mathbb{R}^m) </math> , where {{math|''B''(0,1)}} is the unit ball and <math> W_0^{1,\infty} </math> is the [[Sobolev space]] of essentially bounded functions with essentially bounded derivative and vanishing [[Sobolev_space#Traces|trace]].<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Rindler
 |first=Filip
 |title=Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer International Publishing AG
 |series=Universitext 
 |year=2018
 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-77637-8
 |isbn=978-3-319-77636-1
 |page=106
}}</ref>

==Properties of quasiconvex functions==
*The domain {{math|''B''(0,1)}} can be replaced by any other bounded [[Lipschitz domain]].<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Rindler
 |first=Filip
 |title=Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer International Publishing AG
 |series=Universitext 
 |year=2018
 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-77637-8
 |isbn=978-3-319-77636-1
 |page=108
}}</ref>

*Quasiconvex functions are locally Lipschitz-continuous.<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Dacorogna
 |first=Bernard
 |author-link=Bernard Dacorogna
 |title=Direct Methods in the Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer Science+Business Media, LLC
 |series= Applied mathematical sciences
 |year=2008
 |volume=78
 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-55249-1
 |isbn=978-0-387-35779-9
 |edition= 2nd
 |page=159
}}</ref>

*In the definition the space <math>  W_0^{1,\infty} </math> can be replaced by periodic Sobolev functions.<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Dacorogna
 |first=Bernard
 |author-link=Bernard Dacorogna
 |title=Direct Methods in the Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer Science+Business Media, LLC
 |series= Applied mathematical sciences
 |year=2008
 |volume=78
 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-55249-1
 |isbn=978-0-387-35779-9
 |edition= 2nd
 |page=173
}}</ref>

==Relations to other notions of convexity==
Quasiconvexity is a generalisation of convexity for functions defined on matrices, to see this let <math> A \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d} </math> and <math> V \in L^1(B(0,1), \mathbb{R}^m) </math> with
<math> \int_{B(0,1)} V(x)dx = 0 </math>. The [[Riesz-Markov-Kakutani representation theorem]] states that the [[dual space]] of <math> C_0(\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}) </math> can be identified with the space of signed, finite [[Radon measure]]s on it. We define a Radon measure  <math> \mu </math> by
<math display=block>
\langle h, \mu\rangle = \frac{1}{|B(0,1)|} \int_{B(0,1)} h(A + V(x)) dx
</math>
for <math>h \in  C_0(\mathbb{R}^{m\times d}) </math>. It can be verified that <math> \mu </math> is a
[[probability measure]] and its barycenter is given
<math display="block">
[\mu] = \langle \operatorname{id}, \mu \rangle = A + \int_{B(0,1)} V(x) dx = A.
</math>
If {{math|h}} is a convex function, then [[Jensen%27s_inequality#Proof_2_(measure-theoretic_form)|Jensens' Inequality]] gives
<math display=block>
h(A) = h([\mu]) \leq \langle h, \mu \rangle = \frac{1}{|B(0,1)|} \int_{B(0,1)} h(A + V(x)) dx.
</math>
This holds in particular if {{math|''V''(''x'')}} is the derivative of <math> \psi \in W_0^{1,\infty}(B(0,1), \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}) </math> by the generalised Stokes' Theorem.<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Rindler
 |first=Filip
 |title=Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer International Publishing AG
 |series=Universitext 
 |year=2018
 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-77637-8
 |isbn=978-3-319-77636-1
 |page=107
}}</ref>


The determinant <math> \det \mathbb{R}^{d\times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> is an example of a quasiconvex function, which is not convex.<ref>{{cite book
 |last=Rindler
 |first=Filip
 |title=Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer International Publishing AG
 |series=Universitext 
 |year=2018
 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-77637-8
 |isbn=978-3-319-77636-1
 |page=105
}}</ref> To see that the determinant is not convex, consider
<math display=block>
A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{pmatrix} 
\quad \text{and} \quad
B = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{pmatrix}.
</math>
It then holds <math> \det A = \det B = 0 </math> but for <math> \lambda \in (0,1) </math> we have
<math> \det (\lambda A + (1-\lambda)B) = \lambda(1-\lambda) > 0 = \max(\det A, \det B) </math>. This shows that the determinant is not a [[quasiconvex function|quasiconvex function like in Game Theory]] and thus a distinct notion of convexity.

In the vectorial case of the Calculus of Variations there are other notions of convexity. For a function <math> f: \mathbb{R}^{m\times d} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} </math> it holds that <ref>{{cite book
 |last=Dacorogna
 |first=Bernard
 |author-link=Bernard Dacorogna
 |title=Direct Methods in the Calculus of Variations
 |publisher=Springer Science+Business Media, LLC
 |series= Applied mathematical sciences
 |year=2008
 |volume=78
 |doi=10.1007/978-0-387-55249-1
 |isbn=978-0-387-35779-9
 |edition= 2nd
 |page=159
}}</ref>
<math display=block>
f \text{ convex} \Rightarrow f \text{ polyconvex} \Rightarrow f \text{ quasiconvex} \Rightarrow
f \text{ rank-1-convex}.
</math>

These notions are all equivalent if <math> d = 1 </math> or <math> m=1 </math>. Already in 1952, Morrey conjectured that rank-1-convexity does not imply quasiconvexity.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Morrey 
 |first1=Charles B.
 |author-link=Charles B. Morrey Jr.
 |year=1952
 |title=Quasiconvexity and the Lower Semicontinuity of Multiple Integrals
 |journal=Pacific Journal of Mathematics
 |volume=2
 |issue=1
 |pages=25–53 
 |publisher=Mathematical Sciences Publishers
 |doi=10.2140/pjm.1952.2.25
 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/pacific-journal-of-mathematics/volume-2/issue-1/Quasi-convexity-and-the-lower-semicontinuity-of-multiple-integrals/pjm/1103051941.full
 |access-date=2022-06-30
|doi-access=free
 }}</ref> This was a major unsolved problem in the Calculus of Variations, until Šverák gave an counterexample in 1993 for the case <math> d \geq 2 </math> and <math> m \geq 3 </math>.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Šverák
 |first1=Vladimir
 |author-link=Vladimír Šverák
 |year=1993
 |title=Rank-one convexity does not imply quasiconvexity
 |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of Edinburgh Section A: Mathematics
 |volume=120
 |issue=1–2
 |pages=185–189
 |publisher=	Cambridge University Press, Cambridge; RSE Scotland Foundation
 |doi=10.1017/S0308210500015080
 |s2cid=120192116
 |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/proceedings-of-the-royal-society-of-edinburgh-section-a-mathematics/article/abs/rankone-convexity-does-not-imply-quasiconvexity/2E0BBDE4340DDDDE863F7C365C72C555
 |access-date=2022-06-30
|url-access=subscription
 }}</ref>
The case <math> d = 2</math> or <math> m = 2 </math> is still an [[open problem]], known as Morrey's conjecture.<ref>{{cite journal
 |title= Numerical Approaches for Investigating Quasiconvexity in the Context of Morrey's Conjecture
 |first1=Jendrik |last1=Voss |first2=Robert J. |last2=Martin |first3=Oliver |last3=Sander |first4=Siddhant |last4=Kumar |first5=Dennis M. |last5=Kochmann |first6=Patrizio |last6=Neff
 |journal=[[Journal of Nonlinear Science]] |date= 2022-01-17
 |volume=32 |issue=6 |page=77 |doi=10.1007/s00332-022-09820-x |arxiv= 2201.06392
|bibcode=2022JNS....32...77V |s2cid=246016000 }}</ref>

==Relation to weak lower semi-continuity==
Under certain growth condition of the integrand, the sequential weakly lower semi-continuity (swlsc) of an integral functional in an appropriate Sobolev space is equivalent to the quasiconvexity of the integrand. Acerbi and Fusco proved the following theorem:

'''Theorem:''' If <math> f: \mathbb{R}^d \times \mathbb{R}^m \times \mathbb{R}^{d\times m} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, (x,v,A) \mapsto f(x,v,A) </math> is [[Carathéodory function]] and
it holds <math> 0\leq f(x,v,A) \leq a(x) + C(|v|^p + |A|^p) </math>. Then the functional
<math display=block>
\mathcal{F}[u] = \int_\Omega f(x, u(x),\nabla u(x)) dx
</math>
is swlsc in the Sobolev Space <math> W^{1,p}(\Omega, \mathbb{R}^m) </math> with <math> p > 1 </math>  [[if and only if]] <math> f </math> is quasiconvex. Here <math> C</math> is a positive constant and <math> a(x) </math> an integrable function.<ref>{{cite journal
 |last1=Acerbi
 |first1=Emilio
 |last2=Fusco
 |first2= Nicola
 |author-link2=Nicola Fusco
 |year=1984
 |title=Semicontinuity problems in the calculus of variations
 |journal=Archive for Rational Mechanics and Analysis
 |volume=86
 |issue=1–2
 |pages=125–145
 |publisher=	Springer, Berlin/Heidelberg
 |doi=10.1007/BF00275731
 |bibcode=1984ArRMA..86..125A
 |s2cid=121494852
 |url=https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF00275731
 |access-date=2022-06-30
|url-access=subscription
 }}</ref>

Other authors use different growth conditions and different proof conditions.<ref>{{cite book

 |edition= 2nd

}}</ref> The first proof of it was due to Morrey in his paper, but he required additional assumptions.<ref>{{cite journal
